title: Narada asks for the rules
hookLine: who gets to hand you a mantra? the tradition gives more than one answer, and keeps them all
carry: a mantra is received, not invented

lines: A LINE WHISPERED INTO ONE EAR.
cards: Who gets to hand you a mantra? In one family, a grandfather leans close to a teenager's ear at a ceremony and whispers a line meant for that ear alone, never to be said aloud to friends.
In a park across town, a group sits in a circle singing names of God loud enough for joggers to hear, and anyone who wants to sit down is welcome to join. Both are mantra. Both are japa, in a way.
And both have scripture behind them.

teach.h: DIKSHA: A MANTRA GIVEN BY A GURU.
teach.b: Start with the whisper. In some lineages, a mantra is received from a guru at diksha, initiation. The teacher chooses it and gives it, and the student keeps it private.
The idea is that a mantra given this way carries the teacher's blessing and the lineage's practice behind it; there, picking one off a website isn't the same thing at all. Now the park.
In a short text called the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, the sage Narada asks the god Brahma how to get through the hard age the tradition calls the Kali Yuga.
Brahma answers with a mantra made of the names Hare, Rama and Krishna.

teach.h: NARADA ASKS THE RULES: THERE ARE NONE.
teach.b: Narada asks the obvious follow-up: what are the rules? And Brahma says there are none. Say it, and that's enough.
Some communities point to that line for their open, public chanting. Then there's Om.

teach.h: OM: THE WORD THE VEDAS POINT TO.
teach.b: In the Katha Upanishad, Death himself teaches a boy named Nachiketa that the word all the Vedas point to, the word sought by those who live in discipline, is Om.
And some mantras are drawn from the old texts, like Om namah shivaya, honoring Shiva, whose words namah shivaya appear in the Shri Rudram. So how does someone choose? It depends on the path.
But here's what every answer shares, and it's a real Hindu teaching: a mantra is received, not invented.
The Vedas themselves are called shruti, what was heard, by seers who received them.
A guru passes a mantra on; Brahma gives the names to Narada for everyone. Whichever you receive, the sadhana is to stay with it.

how: In some Hindu lineages a mantra is received privately from a guru at diksha, initiation; in others, such as the public chanting of the divine names, the mantra is open to anyone who wants to say it.

o: chanting every mantra you know, one after another
inventing a new mantra of your own each morning
staying with one mantra that came from a real source

in the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, Narada asks what the rules are
and Brahma answers that there are none.
in the Katha Upanishad, Death teaches Nachiketa about Om
he calls it the word all the Vedas point to.

games.q: you're Narada. Brahma has just given you a mantra of divine names for a hard age. what do you ask next?
o: what the rules for saying it are.
whether anyone else may hear it.
games.why: Narada asks for the rules, and Brahma says there are none: saying the names is enough.

practice: Bring to mind the mantra you chose two days ago, or Om if you haven't chosen, and notice where it came from: a teacher, a family, a text, a temple, a song.
Then begin the japa, silently or in a whisper, one repetition per breath or per bead. If another mantra drifts in, let it pass and come back to the one you chose; staying with one is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, where the mantra comes from: a guru's diksha, the names given for all, or the word the Vedas point to. Received, not invented.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: diksha, initiation, when a guru may give a student a mantra.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: a mantra is received, not invented. A whisper or a park, each one arrives from somewhere. Rest well.
